items: Denaturation: an excess of primers (sequences of 20 to 30 nucleotides) is mixed with the DNA fragment and heated to about 98 C; the double-stranded DNA separates into single strands, each a template for DNA synthesis in vitro.
Annealing of primers: the solution is cooled to about 60 C and the forward and reverse primers anneal (hybridize) to their complementary regions on the single strands.

Extension of primers: the heat-stable Taq polymerase and all four kinds of nucleotide are added; the enzyme adds nucleotides to the 3' end of each primer, copying the rest of the fragment as in replication, so there are now two copies of the original fragment.

Repeating the cycle: steps 1 to 3 are repeated and two copies become four. No more polymerase is needed, because heating does not harm it. Each cycle takes one or two minutes and doubles the DNA; after 20 cycles a single fragment gives more than a million copies.

blocks.alt: A vertical flow. A double-stranded DNA with the gene of interest and free primers (P). Heat: 1- Denaturation separates the strands. Cool: 2- Annealing, a primer P binds to each strand. DNA polymerase (Taq polymerase) and free nucleotides added: 3- Extension builds new strands, giving 2 copies (Cycle 1). Heat and cool again give 4 copies (Cycle 2), then 8 copies (Cycle 3). Old strands are blue, new strands red; the two original strands stay in two of the copies.

blocks.title: For information
blocks.text: The best temperature for extension is 72 C, and this step takes about one minute. Taq polymerase is a temperature-tolerant enzyme from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium of hot springs, and stays stable and active near boiling point. PCR is also used to build genomic libraries, collections of the total DNA of one organism, commonly used for DNA sequencing.

items: Diagnosing infections by detecting the genotypes of infectious agents.
Detecting mutations responsible for some genetic diseases and cancers.
Criminal investigation: 'DNA fingerprints' from cells in a tiny spot of dried blood or at the base of a single hair.
Detecting genetic defects in very early embryos by amplifying the DNA of a few shed cells.
Examining the DNA of extinct species, as long as a minute amount remains intact.
